# UX laws (UX)

This is the short form. Before writing code in this area, read the full rules with reasons, bad/good examples and checks: `.ui-polish/rules/22-ux-laws.md`.

- **UX-01 Fitts's law: important targets are big and close** (warning). Time to hit a target grows with distance and shrinks with size. Make the primary action the largest button in its group, placed where the eye already is: at the end of the form it submits, in the page header for page actions, in a sticky bar on long mobile pages. Pointer targets at least 24px, touch targets 44px (RS-05). Keep destructive actions at least a button's width from frequent ones, never beside Save, and confirm them (NC-07).
- **UX-02 Hick's law: fewer, grouped choices** (warning). Decision time grows with the number of choices. Show at most seven or eight top-level navigation items (group the rest, NV-07), two or three pricing plans with one recommended, one primary and at most two secondary actions per view, and about seven menu options before grouping or adding search (NC-13). Put advanced options behind progressive disclosure.
- **UX-03 Jakob's law: follow the conventions people already know** (warning). Users expect your product to work like the others they use. Keep the conventions: logo top left, linking home; navigation along the top or left; search at the top; account menu and cart top right; links that look like links; a dialog close button at top right plus Escape; the primary dialog button on the right. Break one only with evidence, recorded in `design.md`.
- **UX-04 Miller's law: chunk information** (warning). Working memory holds a handful of items. Chunk anything longer: forms into titled sections of three to seven fields (FM-09), settings into groups, long lists into labelled sections, and long numbers into groups (card numbers in fours, phone numbers by local convention, thousands separators, TY-07). Never make users remember something from a previous screen: repeat it in a summary.
- **UX-05 Von Restorff effect: one thing stands out** (warning). The item that differs is the one noticed. Give each view or region exactly one dominant action (filled primary); make the rest secondary (outline) or tertiary (ghost, link). Mark one recommended pricing plan only. Keep the accent for the one thing needing attention (CO-04), and do not rely on colour alone for the difference (AX-12). If everything is highlighted, nothing is.
- **UX-06 Gestalt: things that look alike behave alike** (warning). People group what looks alike (similarity), what shares a container (common region) and what is close (proximity, SP-03). So: anything that looks like a button acts like one; links share one style; clickable cards have a hover state and an affordance, static cards do not; chips that look alike mean the same thing everywhere; related controls share a container, unrelated ones do not.
- **UX-07 Serial position: first and last are remembered** (info). The first and last items in a series are remembered best. Put the most-used navigation items first and the next most important last; lead sections with the main point and close with the call to action; put the key word first in labels, headings and menu items. Do not bury the item most people need in the middle of a long row.
- **UX-08 Doherty threshold: respond within 400 ms** (warning). Users stay in flow when the interface answers within about 400 ms. Acknowledge every action within 100 ms (pressed state, ST-01) and show a result or progress within 400 ms: a pending button that keeps its width (FM-08), a skeleton (ST-02), or an optimistic update for cheap, reversible actions (ST-06). Past about a second, say what is happening; past ten seconds, show a determinate `<progress>`.
- **UX-09 Goal-gradient and Zeigarnik: show progress toward the goal** (warning). People speed up near a goal and remember unfinished tasks. In any flow longer than one screen, show where the user is and what is left ("Step 2 of 4: Company details" or a labelled `<progress>`), name the next step on the button ("Continue to payment", not "Next"), tick off completed items in setup checklists, and save progress so the flow can be resumed. Merge steps rather than adding them.
- **UX-10 Postel's law: accept input the way people type it** (warning). Be liberal in what you accept, strict in what you store. Accept spaces, dashes and brackets in phone, card, IBAN and postcode fields and strip them before validating; accept emails with surrounding spaces; allow paste everywhere, including password and code fields; never block a keypress. A `pattern` on these fields must allow spaces (for example `[\d ]{13,19}` for card numbers).
- **UX-11 Tesler's law: the product absorbs the complexity** (info). Complexity cannot be removed, only moved: move it into the product. Pre-fill what you know (the user's name and company, country from the locale, today's date, the last-used option), offer defaults most users can accept, infer instead of asking (card type from the number, city from the postcode), and make fields optional where you can (FM-06).
- **UX-12 Peak-end rule: design the best moment and the ending** (info). People judge an experience by its peak and its end. Design the peak of each flow (first invoice sent, order placed): a confirmation that says what happened and offers the next step (ST-05), not a bare "Success". Design the endings too: the last onboarding step, checkout confirmation, cancellation, the 404 page (FD-05). Make the worst moments, errors and failed payments, calm and helpful (CP-05).
